findings.how_to_check: In Stata, run `tab status` and `tab old_cat new_cat if status == "changed"`. Compare `count if status == "net_added"` against the total number of newly added pairs formed by merging the raw pairs on `(histid1930, histid1940)`.
findings.suggested_fix: Either compute pair additions and removals directly at the pair level `(histid1930, histid1940)` so all new pairs appear in Added and all dropped pairs appear in Removed, or clarify the table headers as 'Net Individual Additions/Removals' and add an explicit transition matrix or summary row for partner switches (`status == "changed"`).
findings.title: Added and removed link rows exclude all pairs where a 1930 person's 1940 match changed
findings.what_the_code_does: When comparing a method against Ancestry on 1930 records, the code assigns `status = "changed"` whenever a 1930 record is linked in both sets to different 1940 records (`id_merge == 3 & histid1940_old != histid1940_new`). It categorizes these changed records by truth status into `new_cat` and `old_cat`, but then counts only `status == "net_added"` for `add_*` and `status == "net_removed"` for `rem_*`. The LaTeX table labels these counts 'Added vs. Ancestry: Verified / Unverifiable / Contradicted' and 'Removed vs. Ancestry: Verified / Unverifiable / Contradicted', completely omitting all partner-switched links.
findings.why_it_matters: At the link pair level, switching a 1940 partner removes an old pair and adds a new pair. Omission of 'changed' status conceals substantial pair turnover. More critically, if a new transcription corrects a falsely matched partner (switching from Contradicted to Verified) or introduces an erroneous partner (switching from Verified to Contradicted), that change is invisible in the 'Added' and 'Removed' quality rows. Readers interpreting these rows as accounting for all added or removed links receive an incomplete and biased picture of link quality adjustments.

findings.how_to_check: In `1b_fs_divided_files.do` or by inspecting the intermediate link files, calculate and display the proportion of records and linked pairs where `fs_frst_used == 1` and `fs_last_used == 1` versus where Ancestry fallback was used.
findings.suggested_fix: Report the proportion of links relying on FamilySearch names versus Ancestry fallback in the table or table notes, and report a balanced benchmark restricted to the subsample of records where FamilySearch transcriptions exist for both first and last names in both censuses.
findings.title: FamilySearch benchmark columns evaluate a hybrid Ancestry-fallback policy without reporting coverage
findings.what_the_code_does: The FamilySearch columns in the table (`FS 1930 & 1940`, `FS 1930`, `FS 1940`) are constructed from divided files built in `1b_fs_divided_files.do`, where FamilySearch first and last names are only substituted if `fs_namefrst_cleaned != ""` or `fs_namelast_cleaned != ""`; otherwise, they retain the Ancestry transcription. Although indicators `fs_frst_used` and `fs_last_used` were computed upstream, `score_fs_links.do` drops them and reports linkage performance without indicating what percentage of records actually used FamilySearch names versus falling back to Ancestry.
findings.why_it_matters: FamilySearch transcription availability is non-random and may correlate with record legibility, ethnicity, and linkage difficulty. As a result, differences between Ancestry and 'FamilySearch' columns confound true transcription quality differences with FamilySearch coverage and Ancestry fallback composition. Presenting them alongside pure Ancestry and ML columns without coverage statistics obscures whether improvements stem from FamilySearch transcriptions or from retaining Ancestry where FamilySearch is absent.

findings.how_to_check: Compare the verified match rate and recall of FamilySearch links on an independently constructed linkage benchmark (e.g. hand-linked samples or links established purely through military/vital records independent of census name searches).
findings.suggested_fix: Explicitly qualify in the paper and table notes that the reference link sample is derived from FamilySearch genealogical profiles, and avoid framing agreement with it as absolute 'accuracy' or 'correctness' for the FamilySearch columns without independent validation.
findings.title: Evaluating FamilySearch-name links against FamilySearch-derived profile links is structurally circular
findings.what_the_code_does: The script uses `mlp_training1930_1940.dta` as ground truth (`true_links`), labeling matching links as `Verified Correct` and non-matching links as `Directly Contradicted` or `Unverifiable`. However, `mlp_training1930_1940.dta` was created in `CODE/create_linked_sample_for_MLP_training.do` by merging FamilySearch profile-to-census crosswalks (`unique_ID_to_census_crosswalk1930.dta` and `unique_ID_to_census_crosswalk1940.dta`).
findings.why_it_matters: FamilySearch Family Tree profiles are linked to 1930 and 1940 census records by users and algorithms heavily relying on FamilySearch's proprietary census index and search tools. Evaluating FamilySearch census name transcriptions against links derived from FamilySearch profiles introduces common-source dependency: FamilySearch names will naturally agree more with FamilySearch-generated linkages, mechanically inflating 'Verified Correct' and 'Recall' metrics for FamilySearch columns.

findings.how_to_check: Search the `replication/` directory for `score_fs_links` or `fs_linkage_abe`. Notice zero references. Run `replication/run_machineA.do` and confirm that `MATCHING/results/fs_linkage_abe.tex` is never generated.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `score_fs_links.do` to `replication/run_machineA.do`, register its required input files in `run_machineA.do`'s preflight block, replace the hardcoded path on line 30 with a portable bootstrap, and output the resulting LaTeX table into `$REP_RESULTS`.
findings.title: New FamilySearch scoring script is omitted from replication masters and its multi-gigabyte inputs lack preflight verification
findings.what_the_code_does: The newly introduced script `MATCHING/score_fs_links.do` is not called by `replication/run_machineA.do` or any other master script. Its required multi-gigabyte intermediate inputs (`link1930_1940_fs*.dta`, `divided_file1940_true_cleaned`, `divided_file1930_ans_cleaned`, and `mlp_training1930_1940.dta`) are completely omitted from the preflight checks in `run_machineA.do`. In addition, line 30 contains a hardcoded absolute path `do "D:/repos/fixing_transcription_errors/replication/config.do"`.
findings.why_it_matters: A third party executing the documented replication pipeline (`Run-MachineA.ps1` or `run_machineA.do`) will not produce `MATCHING/results/fs_linkage_abe.tex`. Furthermore, if any of the FamilySearch link files or divided-file directories are missing or corrupted, the failure will not be caught during preflight.

findings.how_to_check: Check whether `histid1930` is uniquely identified before line 240 and line 253 by running `isid histid1930`. If it fails, inspect the duplicate records and check if re-sorting before `duplicates drop` alters the counts.
findings.suggested_fix: Either confirm uniqueness with `isid histid1930` if the link files are guaranteed 1-to-1 on `histid1930`, or define an explicit, deterministic sort order (e.g., `sort histid1930 histid1940`) prior to dropping duplicates, or perform the transition analysis at the pair level.
findings.title: Arbitrary deduplication without sorting makes Panel B link comparison non-deterministic
findings.what_the_code_does: In Part 3, before performing the 1:1 merge on `histid1930`, the code executes `duplicates drop histid1930, force` on `pairs_ans` and `pairs_`c''. There is no preceding `sort` command on either dataset.
findings.why_it_matters: In Stata, `duplicates drop ..., force` without an explicit sort retains the first record encountered in physical storage order. If any 1930 record is associated with multiple 1940 records in `pairs_`c'' (which can occur if ties or multiple candidates survive into the link files), the retained link depends on disk order or prior merge artifacts. This risks non-deterministic results across operating systems, Stata versions, or file rebuilds, and causes Part 3 to evaluate a different link set than Parts 1 and 2 (where duplicates are dropped only on the pair `histid1930 histid1940`).

findings.how_to_check: In the restricted sample, identify records with `status == "net_added"` and check whether their `histid1930` was linked in the full `pairs_ans` file. Tabulate the share of 'net additions' that were actually linked in Ancestry to a congruent record.
findings.suggested_fix: Clearly document in table notes that additions and removals in the restricted sample reflect transitions into and out of the discordant 1940 universe, or condition the comparison on records where the 1930 individual is held constant across both samples.
findings.title: Filtering by 1940 congruence before merging on 1930 ID misclassifies partner switches as sample additions/removals
findings.what_the_code_does: For the restricted sample (`1940 records where Ancestry and FamilySearch disagree`), `pairs_ans` and `pairs_`c'' are separately filtered to keep only pairs where `histid1940` is in `restr1940` (`congruent == 0`). Afterwards, the two sets are merged on `histid1930`.
findings.why_it_matters: If a 1930 person was linked to a concordant 1940 record in Ancestry (`congruent == 1`) but is linked to a discordant 1940 record in New (`congruent == 0`), the record is dropped from Old but retained in New. The merge on `histid1930` then classifies this record as `net_added` rather than a partner switch. Conversely, switching from a discordant to a concordant record is classified as `net_removed`. This confounds sample selection into the discordant subsample with linkage creation and destruction.

review_limits: No paper draft was supplied, so claims-vs-code could not be checked against manuscript prose or published table text; review was limited to code, comments, and the emitted LaTeX table.

The external census microdata and multi-gigabyte link files were not run dynamically through Stata in this sandbox, so runtime execution, exact numerical match rates, and execution speed could not be verified.
The generated output LaTeX table `MATCHING/results/fs_linkage_abe.tex` does not yet exist in the working tree, so rendered layout, compilation, and final formatting could not be visually confirmed.

The exact degree to which the FamilySearch profile links in `mlp_training1930_1940.dta` were created using FamilySearch's census search index depends on external FamilySearch documentation and pipeline code outside the repository.
structured_output.summary: The new scoring script `MATCHING/score_fs_links.do` faithfully implements the paper's ABE calculations and incorporates robust fail-closed checks against baseline figures. However, the evaluation conceals partner-switched links in its added/removed rows, conflates FamilySearch transcription quality with an undocumented Ancestry fallback policy, and evaluates FamilySearch names against a FamilySearch-derived reference. Before submitting, the author should report switched links explicitly, document fallback coverage shares, and integrate the script and its data dependencies into the replication runner.

summary.description: Two to four sentences. The overall state of the reviewed work and the single most important thing to fix. No preamble.

dimensions_reviewed.description: Which scope dimensions were actually reviewed in this run.

findings.description: Defects and concerns, ordered most severe first. Empty if none. Do not pad with stylistic observations.

severity.description: blocker: a reported result is wrong. major: a referee would demand it. minor: real but survivable. nit: cosmetic.

confidence.description: verified: traced in the source. likely: strongly implied but depends on unseen data. speculative: a question, not an established defect.

title.description: One line, stating the defect itself, not its category.

location.description: path:line, or path:line-line. Several may be comma-separated. Required: a finding without a location is not a finding.

what_the_code_does.description: Precisely what the code computes, quoting the relevant expression. Contrast with what it was evidently intended to compute.

why_it_matters.description: The consequence for a number or claim in the paper. If there is no consequence, the severity is nit.

how_to_check.description: A concrete command, tabulation, or count the author can run to confirm or refute this in minutes.

suggested_fix.description: The change, specific enough to act on. Do not apply it yourself.

verified_clean.description: Things explicitly checked that were fine. This is what makes a short findings list trustworthy rather than lazy.

evidence.description: How it was confirmed, with path:line where applicable.

review_limits.description: What this review could NOT establish: data not readable, pipeline not runnable, paper text unavailable, Stata semantics not verifiable by reading. Be explicit; silence here reads as false assurance.
